title: Probability Fundamentals
learning_outcomes: Explain probability Fundamentals and connect at least two of its listed subtopics.
Apply the central idea in probability Fundamentals to a small example or select a suitable approach for a stated scenario.
Identify an important assumption, failure mode, risk, or limitation and describe how it should be checked.

content.intro: In this lesson, you will study probability Fundamentals within Mathematical and Computational Foundations. You will connect the syllabus topics below to a small, inspectable example and practice stating what the evidence does—and does not—support.
content.why_it_matters: Mathematical and computational ideas make model behavior easier to reason about. Start with small values, explicit assumptions, and readable calculations.

content_blocks.title: The central idea
content_blocks.text: Probability describes uncertainty over possible outcomes. Conditional probability depends on the information given, and a probability estimate is meaningful only relative to a defined event and assumptions about the data.

content_blocks.title: Syllabus topics covered in this lesson

items.title: Random variables and outcomes
items.text: Random variables and outcomes is one of the concepts used to reason about probability fundamentals. Define the inputs, assumptions, and intended result in this context, then test the idea on a small representative example and document where it may not apply.

items.title: Probability distributions
items.text: A probability distribution describes how probability is assigned to possible outcomes. Check the support, units, assumptions, and whether the distribution approximates the process that produced the observations.

items.title: Conditional probability
items.text: Conditional probability asks how likely an event is when another event or piece of information is known. It is not interchangeable with the reverse conditional probability.

items.title: Independence
items.text: Independence is one of the concepts used to reason about probability fundamentals. Define the inputs, assumptions, and intended result in this context, then test the idea on a small representative example and document where it may not apply.

items.title: Bayes' theorem
items.text: Bayes’ theorem updates a prior belief using the likelihood of observed evidence to compute a posterior. Be explicit about the event, evidence, and base rate; a high likelihood ratio does not erase a very small prior probability.

items.title: Common probability distributions
items.text: A probability distribution describes how probability is assigned to possible outcomes. Check the support, units, assumptions, and whether the distribution approximates the process that produced the observations.

items.title: Probabilistic reasoning
items.text: Probabilistic reasoning is one of the concepts used to reason about probability fundamentals. Define the inputs, assumptions, and intended result in this context, then test the idea on a small representative example and document where it may not apply.

content_blocks.title: Guided walkthrough
content_blocks.text: 1. Identify what probability fundamentals takes as input and what result or decision it is intended to support. 2. Read the example before running it and predict the output. 3. Run the small example, compare actual and expected output, then change one input or assumption and repeat. 4. Record what the example demonstrates and what it does not demonstrate about a real system.

content_blocks.title: A practical way to reason about it
content_blocks.text: Start with the task definition and the inputs available. Make the expected behavior explicit, choose a simple reference point, and inspect both ordinary examples and cases where assumptions may fail. Mathematical and computational ideas make model behavior easier to reason about. Start with small values, explicit assumptions, and readable calculations.

content_blocks.title: Common mistakes and fixes
content_blocks.text: If the output differs, check indentation and spelling, confirm you saved the intended file, and compare each input value with the example. If the example runs as expected, do not infer that it proves a trained model works; this snippet is a deterministic teaching aid. Keep sensitive data out of tests.

content_blocks.title: Check before you trust a result
content_blocks.text: This is a small, deterministic teaching example—not a trained AI model or evidence of production performance. Run it with a local Python 3 interpreter; do not paste secrets or private data into experiments.

content_blocks.title: Recap and next step
content_blocks.text: Recap: Probability describes uncertainty over possible outcomes. Conditional probability depends on the information given, and a probability estimate is meaningful only relative to a defined event and assumptions about the data. Next, connect this lesson to its prerequisite or next lesson and carry the same habit forward: define success, test a representative case, inspect failures, and document limitations.

content.task: Try it yourself: create a tiny numeric example for probability fundamentals. Write down the variables and units, show the calculation or reasoning step by step, and check the result with a second method or a hand-worked case.
task_acceptance_criteria: Explain the core concept and accurately refer to the source syllabus topics.
Record a prediction and compare it with a reproducible result or a clearly stated manual trace.
Document at least one limitation, safety consideration, or evaluation requirement.
hints: Write down the inputs, expected output, and assumptions before changing the example.
Change only one input or condition and compare the results with your original prediction.
Ask whether the example covers realistic cases, important subgroups, and failure conditions; a toy example does not establish production reliability.
troubleshooting: Use Python 3 and run the file from the folder where it was saved.
If output differs, restore the original input and compare one changed value at a time.
If Python reports a syntax error, check copied quotation marks, indentation, and whether the full code block was copied.
These examples require no external packages, network access, model credentials, or personal data.
